title: The Dan Debate
venue: The Bible and Interpretation (Arizona Center for Judaic Studies)

title: Tel Dan stele: the 'House of David' reading disputed (Stavrakopoulou, quoted)
venue: Wikipedia (open encyclopedia; tertiary, used here only as the open host of the quoted text)

summary: The article quotes F. Stavrakopoulou (2004, p. 86): the 'king of Israel' is secure but 'House of David' is disputed because word dividers appear elsewhere in the inscription and not between byt and dwd. It adds that even if the reading is right it need not show a 9th-century united monarchy, and it records Rainey's reply that dividers are often inconsequential, and a forgery claim by Cryer and Lemche that most scholars rejected.
limits: The quotation is inside a Wikipedia footnote; Stavrakopoulou's book was not opened. Her wording is 'it is disputed', not 'it is wrong'. The forgery charge is rejected by most scholars because the pieces came from controlled excavation.

title: 2 Kings 9:24-27 (Jehu shoots Joram and Ahaziah) read against the Tel Dan claim
venue: Sefaria API, JPS Tanakh 1985 (gender-sensitive ed.)
ask_addressed: Date each inscription with the basis (palaeography, regnal year), the object's location and witness, and the dispute where one exists
quote: King Ahaziah of Judah fled along the road to Beth-haggan. Jehu pursued him and said, "Shoot him down too!"
summary: In 2 Kings 9 it is Jehu who has Joram of Israel and Ahaziah of Judah killed (9:24, 9:27). The Tel Dan speaker (usually Hazael of Damascus) claims in lines 8-9 to have killed a king of Israel and a king of the House of David. The two accounts name different killers; the stele's royal names are themselves restored.
limits: Parallels only; neither text refers to the other. Whether the two accounts conflict, or the stele boasts of a joint war that Jehu then completed, is argued by specialists and I did not open a source that settles it. The identification of the stele's author as Hazael is itself an inference (Hagelia).

summary: Luckenbill's translation of Sennacherib's account of his campaign in Judah: 46 walled cities of Hezekiah taken, 200,150 people carried off, and Hezekiah himself 'like a caged bird' shut up in Jerusalem with earthworks thrown up. title: The Siloam Inscription (PEFQS 1883): the date to be decided on historical, not palaeographical, grounds

Sayce; not relied on). It is included as the earliest documented dating dispute, not as a current view.

title: Radiometric dating of the Siloam Tunnel, Jerusalem
authors: Frumkin, A., Shimron, A., Rosenbaum, J.
ask_addressed: Date each inscription with the basis (palaeography, regnal year), the object's location and witness, and the dispute where one exists
quote: proving its Iron Age II date; we conclude that the Biblical text presents an accurate historic record of the Siloam Tunnel's construction.
summary: Radiocarbon dating of plaster and U-Th dating of stalactites place the tunnel in Iron Age II and the paper says this refutes a claim that it was cut in the second century BCE (the paper's reference list includes Rogerson and Davies 1996, 'Was the Siloam Tunnel built by Hezekiah?', and Hackett et al. 1997, 'The Siloam inscription ain't Hasmonean'; that these are the claim meant is my inference). It dates the tunnel, not the inscription.
limits: Abstract only was read. It measures the tunnel, not the inscription; the identification with Hezekiah is an inference from 2 Kings. The paper's wording 'accurate historic record' goes beyond what a radiometric range of the Iron Age can show.

title: The Lachish Letters: A Reappraisal of the Ostraca Discovered in 1935 and 1938 at Tell ed-Duweir (Lachish 4)
venue: DPhil thesis, University of Oxford (ORA open access), vol. 1

quote: a declaration that the sender and his men are watching the signals of Lachish, but cannot see
summary: Zammit's reappraisal of all 21 Lachish ostraca summarises Lachish 4: a field report that the sender's party is watching the (fire/smoke-)signals of Lachish 'in accordance to all the signs which my lord has given' but cannot see Azekah. Winton Thomas (1945 lecture, opened) dates the letters 'with some reason' to the summer of 589 BCE, 'the last days of Zedekiah'. Whether the sender is at Tell ed-Duweir or another station is itself disputed (Thomas, quoted by Zammit).

title: Aramaic Papyri of the Fifth Century B.C., no. 21: Order to keep the (Passover and) Feast of Unleavened Bread, 419 B.C.
venue: Clarendon Press, Oxford (archive.org scan, public domain)
ask_addressed: Quote the extra-biblical inscriptions and chronicles that bear on Israelite and Judaean history, from open translations
quote: Now this year, the 5th year of King Darius, word was sent from the king to Armies
summary: Cowley's translation of the letter from Hananiah to Yedoniah and 'the Jewish garrison' at Elephantine: word came from King Darius (II) that a festival be kept, with rules for 15th-21st Nisan (Unleavened Bread). Cowley dates it 419 BCE and reads Yedoniah as the community head, as in no. 30. Cowley says the word 'Passover' is only a proposed restoration in the broken lines (see limits).
limits: Half of lines 4-10 are lost. Cowley himself writes 'if the proposed restoration is right, the Passover' and prints '(Passover ?' in his heading; Wikipedia 'Elephantine papyri and ostraca' (opened) says Passover itself 'is not mentioned in the extant text'. So the brief's 'Passover letter' is better described as the Unleavened Bread letter. The royal origin of the instruction is Cowley's reading and the papyrus is not itself a Jerusalem document.

title: Aramaic Papyri of the Fifth Century B.C., no. 30: Petition to the governor of Judaea (Bigvai/Bagohi) for the rebuilding of the temple of Ya'u
venue: Clarendon Press, Oxford (archive.org scan, public domain)
ask_addressed: Quote the extra-biblical inscriptions and chronicles that bear on Israelite and Judaean history, from open translations
quote: The temple of Ya'u the God, which is in the fortress of Yeb let them remove from there.
summary: Yedoniah and the priests at Yeb (Elephantine) petition Bigvai, governor of Judaea, and say they also wrote to Johanan the high priest and 'the nobles of the Jews' in Jerusalem and to the sons of Sanballat, governor of Samaria. They report that the priests of Khnub, with the Persian official Waidrang, had the Yahu temple destroyed in the 14th year of Darius. Cowley dates the letter to the 17th year of Darius II.
limits: Cowley prints 408 BCE for the 17th year of Darius II; Wikipedia 'Elephantine papyri and ostraca' (opened) says the letter was written in 407 BCE, as the brief states. composition.basis: Cowley: 'The date (1. 30) is the 17th year of Darius II = 408 b.c.'; Wikipedia: 'written in 407 BCE'.

text.witness: Papyrus with ll. 1-17 on the recto and ll. 18-30 on the verso, in excellent condition (Cowley); in the Sayce-Cowley collection (Wikipedia); present location not confirmed from an opened source.

strand.to: Judaean governor, Jerusalem high priest and Samaria governors
strand.what: petition for permission to rebuild the temple of Ya'u, showing ties between the Egyptian garrison and Judah's Persian-era authorities
